blocks.text: The concept of entropy was introduced into the study of thermodynamics by Rudolph Clausius in 1856 to give a quantitative basis for the second law. It provides another variable to describe the state of a system, to go along with pressure, volume, temperature and internal energy.

blocks.title: Entropy
blocks.text: If a system undergoes a reversible process during which it absorbs a quantity of heat delta Q at absolute temperature T, the increase in the state variable called the entropy S of the system is delta S = delta Q / T ... (6.8). Like potential energy or internal energy, it is the change in entropy of the system which is important. The change in entropy is positive when heat is added and negative when heat is removed from the system.

Suppose an amount of heat Q flows from a reservoir at temperature T1 through a conducting rod to a reservoir at temperature T2, where T1 is greater than T2. The entropy of the reservoir at T1, which loses heat, decreases by Q/T1, and that of the reservoir at T2, which gains heat, increases by Q/T2. As T1 is greater than T2, Q/T2 is greater than Q/T1; hence the net change in entropy (Q/T2 - Q/T1) is positive. It follows that in all natural processes where heat flows from one system to another there is always a net increase in entropy. This is another statement of the second law of thermodynamics:

blocks.title: Second law in terms of entropy
blocks.text: If a system undergoes a natural process, it will go in the direction that causes the entropy of the system plus the environment to increase.

A natural process tends to proceed towards a state of greater disorder, so there is a relation between entropy and molecular disorder. For example, an irreversible heat flow from a hot to a cold substance of a system increases disorder, because the molecules are initially sorted out in hotter and cooler regions; this order is lost when the system comes to thermal equilibrium. Addition of heat to a system increases its disorder because of the increase in average molecular speeds and therefore the randomness of molecular motion. Similarly, free expansion of a gas increases its disorder because the molecules have greater randomness of position after expansion than before. In both examples the entropy is said to be increased. We can conclude that only those processes are probable for which the entropy of the system increases or remains constant: the process for which entropy remains constant is a reversible process, whereas for all irreversible processes the entropy of the system increases.

Every time entropy increases, the opportunity to convert some heat into work is lost. For example, there is an increase in entropy when hot and cold waters are mixed; finally the warm water cannot be separated into a hot layer and a cold layer. There has been no loss of energy, but some of the energy is no longer available for conversion into work. Therefore an increase in entropy means degradation of energy from a higher level, where more work can be extracted, to a lower level at which less or no useful work can be done: the energy in a sense is degraded, going from a more orderly form to a less orderly form, eventually ending up as thermal energy. In all real processes where heat transfer occurs, the energy available for doing useful work decreases, in other words the entropy increases. Even if the temperature of some system decreases, thereby decreasing the entropy, it is at the expense of a net increase in entropy for some other system; when all the systems are taken together as the universe, the entropy of the universe always increases. (Brain Teaser: why does a deck of cards become more disordered when shuffled?)

blocks.title: Example 6.5
blocks.text: Calculate the entropy change when 1.0 kg of ice at 0 degrees C melts into water at 0 degrees C. Latent heat of fusion of ice L_f = 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1. Solution: m = 1 kg, T = 0 degrees C = 273 K, L_f = 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1. As delta S = delta Q / T, where delta Q = m L_f, delta S = m L_f / T = 1.00 kg x 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1 / 273 K = 1.23 x 10^3 J K^-1. Thus entropy increases as the ice changes to water; the increase in entropy in this case is a measure of the increase in the disorder of the water molecules that change from the solid to the liquid state.

blocks.caption: Entropy at a glance
rows: delta S = delta Q / T for a reversible exchange of heat; a state variable (Clausius, 1856)
positive when heat is added, negative when removed; only the change matters
net change Q/T2 - Q/T1 greater than zero
natural processes raise the entropy of system plus environment; reversible: constant; irreversible: increases
greater molecular disorder; energy degraded, less available for work; the entropy of the universe always increases

blocks.prompt: Calculate the entropy change when 1.0 mole of ice at 0 degrees C melts (numerical 6.6; molar mass 18 g). Explain briefly the heat death of the universe in terms of entropy (short question 6.8).
blocks.explanation: delta S = m L_f / T = 0.018 kg x 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1 / 273 K = 22.2 J K^-1, about 22.0 J K^-1 as printed. Every natural process raises the total entropy, degrading energy to thermal energy at ever more uniform temperature; when all temperature differences have vanished no heat can be turned into work anywhere, the state of maximum entropy pictured as the heat death of the universe.

items: Entropy (Clausius 1856): delta S = delta Q/T, a state variable; + for heat in, - for heat out. Heat Q from T1 to T2 (T1 greater): net entropy change Q/T2 - Q/T1 is positive, so natural processes raise the entropy of the system plus surroundings (second law); constant only for reversible processes.

Entropy measures molecular disorder (heat flow to equilibrium, heating, free expansion); its increase degrades energy, less of it available for work; the entropy of the universe always increases. Example 6.5: 1 kg of ice melting gains 1.23 x 10^3 J K^-1.
